title: SMART Goes Live in Washington Today — and the More Important Question Is Whether Airlines' Flight Planning Systems Are Ready to Receive It
summary: The FAA's SMART air traffic management system begins its first operational trial today in the Washington, D.C. area — a milestone that raises an immediate question about how its route and timing outputs actually reach the cockpit.
body_markdown:
I've covered the SMART program twice before — when the FAA awarded the contract to Air Space Intelligence in June, and again when airlines flagged data-sharing concerns in Senate testimony. Today is a genuinely different moment: the system appears to be going live.

## What's Actually Happening

<cite index="28-1,28-3">The FAA is preparing to put SMART, its new predictive traffic-planning software, into operational use in the Washington area — what would be the system's first operational fielding.</cite> <cite index="30-3">SMART — Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — sits under a 12-year, $875-million contract with Air Space Intelligence, and is designed to support both the FAA and airlines with operations, schedules, and reducing delays and cancellations.</cite> <cite index="29-13">The first roughly 90-day test will help determine how well the system works before any wider rollout.</cite>

The press framing on this has been predictably focused on the ATC side: controllers getting a smarter picture, congestion predicted before it develops. That's real, but it's also not the whole story.

## The Part That Affects Flight Planning Directly

<cite index="28-9">FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told a House appropriations subcommittee on September 15 that SMART uses AI to predict congestion and conflicts earlier, "adjusting departure times, routes, and timing at designated points enroute."</cite> Those aren't abstract ATM outputs — those are the same variables sitting inside every airline's flight plan. Departure time adjustments, reroutes, and enroute timing constraints are precisely what dispatchers and pilots are working from when they file and brief.

<cite index="36-2,36-3">SMART is designed to give air traffic managers a more comprehensive picture by combining airline schedules, weather forecasts, airport runway capacity, airspace restrictions, and other operational information — and rather than waiting until congestion has already disrupted flights, it's built to identify potential problems earlier and provide options for resolving them.</cite> That earlier identification window is where the cockpit angle becomes interesting. If SMART is generating route alternatives or departure time adjustments ahead of the gate, the downstream question is how quickly those recommendations propagate into the flight planning tools a crew is actually looking at during preflight.

<cite index="28-10">SMART sits inside FMDS — the Flow Management Data and Services platform the FAA selected Air Space Intelligence to build.</cite> FMDS is the architectural layer that's supposed to modernize how traffic management data flows between the FAA and airline operations systems. The quality of that data feed, and how cleanly it interfaces with downstream flight planning software, is going to determine whether SMART's earlier-detection capability actually translates into better information on the flightdeck — or stays contained inside the ATCSCC.

## The 90-Day Trial as a Calibration Moment

<cite index="30-4">Reports emerged of concerns from officials at three airlines who wanted to reduce the scope of the project with a "start, crawl, walk, run" approach</cite> — and that caution is probably well-placed, for reasons that have less to do with AI skepticism and more to do with integration reality. Plugging a new predictive layer into the flow management stack without disrupting the data contracts that airline flight planning vendors rely on is genuinely hard, and the 90-day Washington trial is as much a test of that integration surface as it is a test of the AI.

<cite index="30-5">The advent of the SMART system has been hailed by Airlines for America as "one of the most exciting and bold initiatives taken on by the FAA in decades."</cite> That kind of enthusiasm is worth tempering slightly — not because the system isn't promising, but because the proof will be in what airline flight planning platforms can actually consume from it, and how quickly.

From time spent on the delivery side of aviation software programs, I'd say the pipeline between an ATM system's output and what appears in a flight planning tool is where the most implementation surprises tend to surface. The Washington trial starting today is the moment that pipeline gets its first real-world test.

email_brief: The FAA's SMART system — built by Air Space Intelligence under an $875M, 12-year contract — is beginning its first operational trial today (September 21) in the Washington, D.C. area, covering the three major airports there. Prior posts covered the contract award and Congressional testimony about data-sharing concerns; this is the system actually going live for the first time. The story is framed in today's post around the flight planning data pipeline question: SMART generates route and departure time adjustments that need to propagate downstream into airline flight planning tools, and the 90-day trial is as much a test of that integration surface as it is a test of the AI. The cockpit relevance is direct — SMART's outputs are the same variables pilots and dispatchers work from in preflight planning.
